data.text:
BREAKING: Iranian drones struck a fuel storage tank at Kuwait International Airport shortly after 2am local time this morning. Fire broke out. Firefighting teams contained it. No casualties. Kuwait Civil Aviation Authority confirmed the strike and activated emergency measures.

This is not the first time. The same fuel tanks were hit on March 8. The same airport. The same time of night. The same outcome: fire, containment, no deaths. The repetition is not failure. It is calibration. The IRGC is not trying to destroy Kuwait International Airport. It is demonstrating that it can reach the fuel supply of every aircraft that operates from it, whenever it chooses, as many times as it chooses, and nobody can stop the drone from arriving.

Kuwait hosts Ali Al Salem Air Base, Camp Arifjan, Camp Buehring, and the Shuaiba port logistics hub. These are not Kuwaiti facilities with American visitors. They are the forward operating infrastructure of the United States military in the Persian Gulf. Ali Al Salem launches the sorties. Camp Arifjan coordinates the logistics. Shuaiba receives the supplies. And Kuwait International Airport’s fuel tanks, operated by Kafco and fed by pipelines from Mina al-Ahmadi and Mina Abdullah refineries, supply the jet fuel that keeps everything in the air.

When you hit the fuel tank at 2am, you are not hitting the airport. You are hitting the supply chain that connects refineries to runways to combat aircraft to Iranian airspace. The IRGC does not need to destroy the runway. It needs to demonstrate that the fuel sitting on the runway can burn at any time. The demonstration is the weapon. The repetition is the proof that air defences cannot guarantee the fuel supply. And every Patriot interceptor fired at a $20,000 Shahed drone costs $3 million. The arithmetic of attrition favours the drone.

Kuwait’s Emir called the strikes “unprovoked.” Kuwait has publicly denied allowing US offensive operations from its soil. But IRGC targeting calculus does not distinguish between active participation and passive hosting. If American aircraft launch from your territory, your fuel tanks are part of the supply chain. If American logistics flow through your ports, your ports are targets. Iran’s position, stated explicitly by Araghchi, is that countries “that have given their soil to American forces to attack us” are legitimate targets regardless of their stated neutrality. The neutrality is diplomatic. The geography is military. And the drones read geography.

The pattern since February 28 tells the story. Airport fuel tanks, refinery approaches, power lines, base perimeters. Seven overhead power lines taken offline in a single night. Radar installations. Terminal buildings. Each strike is low-casualty, contained, repairable. Each strike is also unrepeatable proof that the IRGC can reach the target again. The message to Kuwait is not “we will destroy you.” The message is “we can touch you, and the Americans cannot prevent it, and you should ask them to stop the war before we touch something that does not contain.”

The message to Washington is different but related. Every drone that reaches a fuel tank in Kuwait is a drone that air defences did not intercept. Every unintercepted drone is evidence that the defensive umbrella has gaps. Every gap is a planning variable for the next wave. And the waves come at 2am, when the message arrives before the morning briefing.

So many countries now absorbing the consequences of a 21-mile strait: Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, Slovenia, South Korea, Philippines, United Kingdom, Kuwait and many others globally. The list grows. The fuel burns. The drones arrive. The molecules remain trapped.

🇺🇸🇮🇷🇮🇱 - WAR IN IRAN | MARCH 24th, DAY 25 RECAP:

🇮🇷🇮🇱 - Multiple Iranian missile attacks on Israel throughout the day caused dozens of injuries and damage to buildings. “The home of Knesset member Meirav Ben-Ari was destroyed by an Iranian missile this morning,” according to Israeli media.

🇸🇦🇦🇪🇮🇷 - "Riyadh seeks to re-establish deterrence and is nearing a decision to join the war on Iran. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are considering joining the fight after recent Iranian attacks on their energy infrastructure," The Wall Street Journal reports. Saudi Arabia denied this report and said it seeks an end to the war.

🇮🇷🇮🇱 - Iran has used a new type of missile or warhead in its attack on Tel Aviv. It reportedly launched a single missile carrying 3–4 bombs, each weighing around 100 kg, causing significant damage to at least three buildings, according to Israeli officials.

🇰🇷🇴🇲 - South Korea’s Foreign Minister Cho asked his Omani counterpart for support with crude oil and LNG supplies during a phone call due to the effects of the Iran war.

🇺🇸🇵🇭🛢 - The Philippines is working with Washington to secure waivers and exemptions so it can buy oil from U.S.-sanctioned countries, Philippines Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez told Reuters.

🇮🇱 - An IDF reserve soldier was found dead after shooting himself in the head inside a shelter in Bat Yam, Israel.

🇮🇷🇮🇱 - Iran launched seven waves of missile attacks at Israel over a span of ten hours last night, according to CNN.

🇮🇷 - Iran has appointed former IRGC commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr as secretary of Iran’s National Security Council, replacing Ali Larijani. Zolghadr is a known IRGC hardliner; he was said to be so hardline that Qassem Soleimani briefly left the IRGC due to repression he witnessed from figures like Zolghadr.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - Marco Rubio will attend a G7 meeting on the topic of Iran this Friday.

🇶🇦🇮🇷 - QatarEnergy has declared force majeure on certain affected long-term LNG supply contracts, impacting customers in Italy, Belgium, South Korea, and China, Reuters reports.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - Ali Akbar Ahmadian, a former IRGC commander best known as an architect of Iran’s asymmetric warfare strategy, said they have been waiting for years for an American ground invasion and urged them to “come closer.”

🇺🇸🇮🇱🇮🇶 - The Iraqi Armed Forces and the Iraqi Council of National Security have given the Popular Mobilization Forces full authority to respond to and retaliate against any U.S. and Israeli attacks, effectively giving them the green light to formally enter the war—a stunning declaration.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - An American 15-point ceasefire plan, first reported by Israeli Channel 12, was presented to Iran via Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir, who has a close relationship with both the Iranian IRGC and President Trump. Officials say it is unlikely Iran will respond soon, according to The New York Times.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - Saeed Jalili, a member of Iran’s Expediency Discernment Council and a known hardliner, said the United States has gone from openly discussing regime change to now hoping Iran will engage in dialogue, adding that this is merely deception.

🇻🇦 - Pope Leo XIV has called for a ceasefire and urged all parties engaged in the Iran war to seek peace through talks.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 - Iran refuses to negotiate with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and prefers JD Vance, according to CNN.

🇮🇷🇰🇼 - Drones struck fuel tanks at Kuwait International Airport, causing a large fire, according to Kuwait’s General Civil Aviation Authority.

🇺🇸🇮🇷🇮🇱 - Iranian demands to end the war, according to The Wall Street Journal: Closure of all American bases in the Gulf. A new order for the Strait of Hormuz allowing Iran to collect fees from ships transiting the waterway, similar to the Suez Canal. Guarantees that the war would not restart and an end to Israel’s strikes on the Iran-aligned Lebanese militia Hezbollah. Lifting all sanctions on Iran. Permitting Iran to keep its missile program with no negotiations to limit it.

My objective take on the question: Is the country currently in a CRISIS or rather under PRESSURE? (to date)

Global standards are clear. 
The International Monetary Fund defines a crisis as severe economic disruption , marked by contraction, high inflation, or external imbalance. 
The World Bank adds that crisis occurs when economic stress, institutional strain, and threats to basic needs happen at the same time. 
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development frames it as systemic failure across economic, political, and social dimensions.

Applied to the Philippines today, those thresholds are not met.
Yes, the Middle East conflict is pushing oil prices higher. Inflation risks are rising, and transport sectors feel the strain. But fuel remains available, the economy continues to grow, and government responses are active.

By global standards, a crisis is not rising pressure, it is system breakdown.

The Philippines today is strained, but still functioning, not technically in crisis.

#PhilippinesEnergy #FuelPricePressure
